transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, to be completely honest with you, I wouldn't even be here if it were up to me. It was the occupational health department at my plant that forced the issue. I work in metal fabrication, you know, running the heavy presses, moving materials around all day—it's a very physical job, and you have to be sharp, which I am. I've been doing it a long time. 

But we had our mandatory health screenings the other day, and the nurse there... well, she made this absolute mountain out of a molehill during my weigh-in. She looked at the scale, looked at me, and basically told the floor manager that my weight is—and this is her exact phrasing—dangerously low for someone doing fabrication and running presses all day. Which I just think is a massive overreaction. I mean, I’ve just been really focusing on my routine lately, and I honestly thought I was just getting leaner. You know, shedding the excess so I can be more disciplined, more efficient on the floor. I've been working so hard on that discipline. But now they’re making me jump through all these hoops and come see you before they'll clear me to go back to my station, which is just incredibly frustrating because I'm just trying to do my job and they're acting like I'm about to break in half or something.
Have you noticed any unintentional weight loss recently, or has your weight loss been entirely due to your focused efforts on routine and discipline?

No, no, it's not unintentional at all. It's completely intentional. I mean, I don't just lose weight by accident, you know? It takes a lot of effort and, like I said, discipline. It's all very calculated. I have to be so careful because if I'm not, everything just feels... chaotic. So, I have this whole system down now. Most days, I just have a black coffee before my early shift—I have to be on the floor by 6:00 AM, so the coffee just wakes me up and keeps me focused without feeling heavy. And then, at lunch, when everyone else is eating these huge sandwiches from the canteen, I just have maybe half of a protein bar. Just enough to get through the rest of the shift, you know? Because if I eat more than that, I start feeling sluggish on the presses, and I can't afford to be sluggish. Then, after work, I go straight to my yoga class, which is essential for stretching out my back after being on the concrete floor all day, and when I finally get home, I just have a small bowl of steamed vegetables. That's it. That's all I need. Honestly, if I eat more than that... if I deviate from that plan, the whole day just feels completely out of control. Like I've failed. So, yes, it's very intentional. I've worked really hard to get my intake exactly where I want it.
Do you feel that your weight or the way your body looks has an unusual impact on how you see yourself or your sense of self-worth?

Well... I mean, I guess it does. A lot, actually. Because, well, for example, we have these really harsh, just awful fluorescent lights in the women's locker room at the plant. And when I'm changing into or out of my work gear—my heavy boots and my protective stuff—I'll catch sight of myself in the bathroom mirror over the sinks. And the moment I do, it's just... it's all I can focus on. My stomach and my thighs, they just look so big to me. 

It's the same thing if I'm walking to the bus stop after my shift and I happen to see my reflection in one of the shop windows downtown. I'll just catch a glimpse, and all I can see is how wide my thighs look, or how my stomach isn't flat enough. And honestly, it completely ruins how I feel about myself for the rest of the entire day. I'll just spiral. I'll spend hours thinking about it, feeling just... disgusted, I guess? Like I'm a total failure. 

Because I put in all this intense effort, all this discipline with my routine that I was just telling you about, and then I see that reflection and it just wipes out any sense of accomplishment or worth I had. It dictates my entire mood. Like, I can't even focus on relaxing or unwinding after a long shift on the presses because I'm just sitting there thinking about how big I looked in that window, and wondering why I can't just get it right. It just hangs over me like this heavy dark cloud, and I can't shake the feeling that if my body looks like that, then I'm just not trying hard enough, which makes me feel incredibly guilty and weak. So, yeah, it definitely impacts how I see myself. Probably more than it should, but I just can't turn it off once I see it.
Do you have a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even if others might see you as underweight or too thin?

Oh, absolutely. It’s... honestly, it’s a constant, overwhelming fear. Like, I have this digital scale in my bathroom, the kind that measures down to the exact tenth of a pound, and every single morning, right after I wake up—before I even have that black coffee I told you about, before I even take a shower or brush my teeth—I step on it. And if that number goes up... I mean, even if it’s just by a tiny fraction, like point-two of a pound, I just feel this absolute, blinding panic wash over me. 

My heart starts pounding and my chest gets tight, because all I can think is that I’m losing my grip. I've spent so much time and energy getting everything so perfectly calibrated, and if the scale goes up even a little, I panic that I’m going to lose all the control I’ve worked so incredibly hard for. It feels like if I let it slide even a fraction of an inch, if I accept even a tiny gain, then the whole system is just going to completely collapse. I’ll just keep gaining and gaining, and I'll end up heavy again. And I just can't go back to that. I can't. 

People at the plant, like that occupational health nurse, they might look at me and decide I'm too thin or whatever, but they don't understand how quickly it can all fall apart. They don't see the mental math I have to do every single second of the day just to keep myself from spiraling. They don't understand that the control is the only thing keeping me functioning on the floor, keeping me sharp enough to run those heavy presses safely. So yes, the thought of gaining weight, of seeing that number climb and knowing I've failed... it terrifies me. I just can't let myself lose this control and get heavy again.
